name: master-slave
intent: Deliver one service request through a set of semantically identical workers that a single master partitions, dispatches and recombines, so the service gains speed, redundancy or computational accuracy without its clients knowing that the work was ever split.
problem: A service must be delivered by splitting its work into sub-tasks (parallel speedup), by executing it several times (fault tolerance or numerical accuracy), or both - yet clients must keep seeing one operation, the sub-task implementations must stay interchangeable and independent of how work is partitioned and results are combined, and some coordination instance has to divide the work, hand it out, and merge the partial results.
context: Work that factors into independent sub-tasks: multicore hosts, clusters, grids and worker fleets running matrix and vector computations, randomized search, batch jobs, replicated controllers. The pattern assumes sub-tasks exchange little or no state while they run; if the parts must communicate continuously, data-parallel or domain decomposition with a shared-memory model fits better. The master may be a thread, a process, a rank-0 node or a service in front of a worker pool, and the sub-task transfer may be a call parameter, a work queue or a shared repository.
benefits: Scalability without changing the service interface: more workers shorten the wall-clock time while clients still call one operation (POSA1 lists this transparency as a force - neither clients nor the sub-task processing should depend on how work is partitioned and combined).
One sub-service, many workers: partition and combine logic is written once and reused, so capacity is added by replicating a homogeneous unit rather than by special-casing the service.

Three applications from one structure: parallel computing, fault tolerance through replicated execution with voting, and computational accuracy through semantically identical but independently written implementations.
Load adaptation when workers pull from a shared work pool: heterogeneous or drifting processors balance themselves instead of depending on a static equal partition.
Location independence: slaves can run on other cores, machines or nodes; only the sub-task interface and the partial results cross the boundary.
Failure containment per sub-task: independent sub-tasks mean a failed or restarted worker normally costs only its own partial result, provided the master defines the failure policy.
The sub-tasks are directly testable in isolation, and a single worker can be profiled or replaced without touching the clients.
tradeoffs: The master is the central coordination point and therefore the throughput ceiling: when dispatch or result traffic grows with the number of workers, the single master or the shared link saturates before the workers do (POSA1's travelling-salesman example rejected one shared graph precisely because the network load would have dominated).
A single master is also a single point of failure, which undermines the fault-tolerance application unless the coordinator itself is replicated or checkpointed.

Failure and cancellation policy becomes part of the design: a dead worker must not block the master forever, a slow straggler idles the rest unless work is pulled from a queue, and late or partial results must be discarded or retried explicitly.
Task granularity is a new tuning parameter: too few sub-tasks leave workers idle, too many make dispatch, serialization and result copying exceed the useful computation.
Results must be combined deterministically and independently of arrival order, and sub-tasks must be free of hidden shared state - workers that mutate their inputs need private copies.

Replicated execution buys accuracy only while failures are uncorrelated: running one implementation several times cannot detect deterministic bugs, and the master needs a documented voting or comparison rule.
Debugging, tracing and profiling span threads, processes or hosts, and exceptions must be marshalled back to the master explicitly instead of unwinding through a shared stack.
More moving parts than a plain parallel loop: client, master, sub-service interface and worker set all need interfaces plus a lifecycle and shutdown discipline.

participants.responsibility: Calls the service as one operation and remains unaware of how the request is partitioned, dispatched and recombined.
Divides the request into independent sub-tasks, dispatches them to workers, waits for or monitors them, and computes the final result from the partial results returned.
Semantically identical worker that executes one sub-task through the sub-service interface, owns no shared mutable state, and returns a partial result to the master or to a result repository.
Contract defining a sub-task and its partial result; it keeps the master independent of concrete worker implementations and lets deliberately different implementations run side by side for accuracy.

Optional hand-off structure (queue, channel, tuple space, blackboard) that decouples dispatch from execution: workers pull sub-tasks and/or deposit partial results, enabling dynamic balancing (the workpool variant).

use_cases: Data-parallel numeric work with a natural unit per worker: matrix multiplication by rows, transform coding of an image block by block, cross-correlation by partitions of the sample stream (the three examples POSA1 attributes to [KSS96]).

Approximate search and randomized algorithms: each worker explores a random subset of a huge search space, such as candidate routes for the travelling-salesman problem, and the master keeps the best result found.

Replicated execution for fault tolerance or accuracy: several workers run the same sub-service and the master compares or votes over the results (triple modular redundancy, diverse implementations for numerical accuracy).

Batch and grid processing: a scheduling process splits a job into tasks and distributes them to worker processes or nodes - build farms, render farms, test shards, and the map step of MapReduce with the master as combiner.

Service-side fan-out: a request handler splits an aggregate query or a set of independent downstream calls into sub-requests handled by worker threads or services, then merges the responses (scatter-gather).
Multi-phase simulation where sub-tasks occasionally need coordination between phases: the master, not the workers, sequences the phases and exchanges boundary data.

GPU kernel dispatch: a CUDA or OpenCL host program acts as master, partitions a grid into blocks and streams them to device worker cores, then synchronises and copies results back — the device is a tightly-coupled slave pool behind a PCIe boundary.

Distributed compilation and build farms: a build coordinator (master) distributes translation units to compiler worker processes across a cluster; each worker produces an object file and the master links the final binary, as in Bazel's remote build system or distcc.

Parameter sweeps and scientific Monte Carlo simulations: the master partitions a parameter space into independent trials and farms each trial to a worker process or node; results are aggregated into a summary statistic (mean, confidence interval) upon completion.

Apache Hadoop MapReduce: the ResourceManager and per-application MRAppMaster schedule mapper and reducer tasks on NodeManagers, while the job client observes one submitted job and receives the aggregated result.

OpenMP's parallel-for/worksharing-loop construct: the runtime master distributes loop iterations to a team of worker threads, with static, dynamic or guided schedules selecting equal or pull-like task assignment.

Python's concurrent.futures Executor family: ThreadPoolExecutor or ProcessPoolExecutor accepts submitted callables through one interface, runs them in a bounded worker pool, and exposes Future results and exceptions for the coordinating caller.
avoid_when: The decomposition is recursive with a natural combine step and irregular load: fork/join with a work-stealing pool expresses that with less ceremony than a fixed worker set.

The work is uniform and data-parallel over a collection: a parallel loop or parallel collection (parallelStream, par_iter, OpenMP parallel for) removes the explicit master with less code and better balancing.
Parts must exchange fine-grained state while they run: a shared-memory parallel algorithm, domain decomposition or a streaming/actor model fits, because master-slave assumes independent sub-tasks.
There is no real parallelism to win - a single core, or sub-tasks smaller than the dispatch and serialization overhead: sequential code is faster and simpler.

The runtime already supplies the worker set for this problem class (a job framework, a queue-backed worker service, a parallel query engine, a platform scheduler): adding a master role duplicates the scheduler.
The workload is unbounded and streaming: a producer/consumer or actor pipeline with backpressure is simpler than repeated master-driven rounds.
The term is meant as database replication (primary and replicas): that is a data-replication concern with its own failure and consistency rules, not this computational pattern.
anti_patterns: The master that also performs worker tasks: the coordinating role becomes the critical path and the decomposition loses the parallelism it was introduced for.
One thread or process per sub-task instead of a bounded worker set: creation and teardown cost more than the work and the machine oversubscribes.
Static equal partitions over sub-tasks with very different costs: the fastest workers idle while one straggler decides the wall-clock time.
Workers writing into shared mutable result state without synchronization or a deterministic combination order, so the result depends on scheduling.
Deploying a single master as the fault-tolerance mechanism: the coordinator has no replica, so worker faults are converted into system outages.
Copying one deterministic bug into every replica and calling it redundancy: without independent implementations or a voting rule nothing is detected.
Silent workers - no timeout, no error channel, no completeness count - so one dead worker turns the whole service into a hang.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: partition, dispatch and combine (master) versus sub-task processing (workers).
Information hiding: clients and workers see only the service operation and the sub-service interface, never the partitioning or combination logic.
Dependency inversion: the master depends on the sub-service abstraction, so worker implementations stay interchangeable - and can differ deliberately for accuracy.
Single responsibility and symmetry: the master coordinates, every worker is an equivalent instance with identical responsibilities; there is no leader among the workers.
Open/closed principle: new sub-task algorithms, hardware or nodes arrive behind the sub-service interface without edits to the master's clients.
best_practices: Derive granularity from measured sub-task cost, and prefer pulling from a work queue over a static equal split whenever costs vary.
Keep the worker set bounded and reusable; never create a worker per sub-task.
Specify the master's failure policy: timeouts, retry or re-dispatch, a completeness count, and defined behaviour when a worker dies or returns late.
Keep sub-tasks independent: copy inputs that workers mutate and forbid hidden shared state between workers.
Combine partial results deterministically, in a defined order and independently of completion order.
Preserve the client illusion - one operation, one result - because the decomposition is an implementation detail.
For replicated execution use genuinely independent implementations where accuracy is the goal, and a documented voting rule (majority, quorum) where fault tolerance is the goal.
Instrument the master: per-worker throughput, queue depth and straggler detection show when the coordinator or the granularity is the bottleneck.

Prefer a work-pool (pull) variant over push dispatch when sub-task costs are unknown or heterogeneous: workers grab the next task on completion, so fast workers automatically take more work without the master having to predict runtimes.

Size the worker pool to the parallelism available (CPU cores, GPU streams, network connections) and add headroom for blocking: an I/O-bound workload needs more workers than cores, but a CPU-bound workload saturates at core count.

Make sub-tasks idempotent and the master's completion policy explicit: mark tasks complete on first result, or collect all and reduce, or take majority vote — document which and enforce it with a completeness counter.

Marshal exceptions across process or network boundaries explicitly: uncaught exceptions in a worker process are silently swallowed unless the master installs an exception handler or the framework (concurrent.futures, ExecutorService) propagates them via Future.exception().
sources: Buschmann, Meunier, Rohnert, Sommerlad & Stal, Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 1: A System of Patterns (Wiley, 1996) - Master-Slave (Design Patterns chapter, p. 245): a master divides work into sub-tasks, delegates them to independent but semantically identical slaves, and computes the final result from the partial results they return; application areas are fault tolerance, parallel computing and computational accuracy.

https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html — Python standard library documentation for concurrent.futures, describing ProcessPoolExecutor and ThreadPoolExecutor as explicit worker-pool (task-farm) abstractions; the execute() method on each worker is the sub-service interface.

https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/util/concurrent/ExecutorService.html — Oracle Java 8 API documentation for ExecutorService, the central abstraction in Java's Fork/Join framework that realises a master-worker topology via submit() and invokeAll() with a configurable worker pool.

https://go.dev/blog/pipelines — 'Go Concurrency Patterns: Pipelines' (official Go Blog), demonstrating fan-out (master distributes to concurrent goroutine workers) and fan-in (results are combined); the worker goroutines are stateless and return results via channels.

https://www3.nd.edu/~dthain/patterns/ — Douglas Thain's 'Design Patterns for Parallel Computing' (University of Notre Dame), a widely-cited academic survey that covers the Master-Worker pattern with pseudocode, performance analysis, and references to POSIX threads and MPI implementations.

http://hillside.net/master-slave — Hillside.net pattern catalog entry for Master-Slave, providing a cross-language summary, relationships to other patterns, and known uses in embedded systems and telecommunications.

https://www.openmp.org/spec-html/5.0/openmpsu41.html — OpenMP 5.0 Specification §1.3 (parallel construct) and §2.9.5.1 (schedule clause): the 'parallel for' directive creates an implicit master that distributes loop iterations to a team of worker threads; the schedule(static) variant is an equal-split master-slave, schedule(dynamic) is a work-pool variant.

https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/pattern-oriented-software-architecture/9781119963998/chap18-sec001.html — canonical POSA-oriented definition: a master divides work into identical sub-tasks handled by interchangeable slaves while clients remain unaware of the decomposition.
https://openmp.org/spec-html/5.1/openmpsu73.html — OpenMP 5.1 parallel worksharing-loop construct, where a team of worker threads receives loop iterations under explicit scheduling policies.

https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html — Python's official Executor, ThreadPoolExecutor and ProcessPoolExecutor worker-pool interfaces, including Future result and exception handling.
https://go.dev/blog/pipelines — official Go fan-out/fan-in pipeline guidance showing workers consuming shared input and a coordinator merging outputs with cancellation.

https://hadoop.apache.org/docs/current3/hadoop-mapreduce-client/hadoop-mapreduce-client-core/MapReduceTutorial.html — Apache Hadoop MapReduce job submission, scheduling, monitoring and mapper/reducer worker execution.

https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/architectural-patterns/9781787287495/9af9516f-f167-46bc-8fd8-01088c24f2c9.xhtml — discussion of master-slave liabilities, including central coordination bottlenecks and the master's single-point-of-failure risk.
pitfalls: Result-size explosion: if partial results are large (e.g. per-partition intermediate data), serialising and copying them back to the master dominates the wall-clock time; use a result repository the master reads from instead of materialising results in messages.

Straggler amplification: in a synchronous wait (invokeAll / wait()), the overall job is held by the single slowest sub-task; use asynchronous collection with a timeout and re-dispatch policy to mitigate one pathological worker.

Master coordination overhead: when sub-tasks are very fine-grained (sub-millisecond), the dispatch-deserialize-execute-serialise-return cycle costs more than the work itself; merge multiple micro-tasks into a coarse batch per worker.

Silent task loss under backpressure: if a push-based master fires tasks faster than workers can absorb them and the queue is bounded, overflow drops tasks silently unless the master implements explicit acknowledgement or an unbounded work-pool variant.

Worker pool starvation under priority inversion: a long-running low-priority sub-task can hold a worker slot while a high-priority task waits in the queue; use separate pools or priority-aware scheduling to prevent priority inversion.

Non-deterministic combine when results are stateful: if partial results depend on mutable shared read-only state that changes between workers' runs, the combined output varies even for identical seeds; freeze inputs or make copies explicit.

Checkpoint overhead misjudged: checkpointing the master for fault tolerance adds synchronous I/O on the critical path; if sub-task durations are short, checkpoint cost exceeds the cost of simply re-running the failed sub-task.

Wrong move: Treat a queue-backed scheduler as master-slave merely because it has workers -> the pattern claim fails when no coordinator partitions one client-visible operation and combines its partial results -> instead model the scheduler as infrastructure and name the master-slave boundary explicitly.

Wrong move: Add workers indefinitely behind one master -> throughput fails when dispatch, result traffic or serial reduction saturates the coordinator -> instead measure coordination cost and shard or hierarchize the coordinator when it becomes the bottleneck.

Wrong move: Replicate identical workers and call it fault tolerance -> the vote fails when a deterministic defect or correlated failure appears in every replica -> instead use independent implementations or failure domains plus an explicit quorum or voting rule.
